1961.heavy: Not weight: the stress-attracting property is tone. Ranked by P&P: HL sequence > ML sequence > bare H > first couplet syllable; by de Lacy: HL > H > ML > leftmost. Syllables are (C)(C)V(?) with no codas and no weight contrast (Herrera: (C)V syllables, bimoraic minimal word, glottal closure contrastive and independent of accent). P&P: post-couplet CV vowels are shorter than couplet vowels and pre-couplet syllables 'have no stress, and their vowels have shorter allophones' -- length is a correlate of stress, not a conditioning weight.
1961.dflt: First syllable of the couplet (= leftmost syllable of the root + suffix domain) when the word has no high tone and no ML sequence: 'if there is no tone 1, then it occurs on the first syllable of the couplet' (P&P 1967: 293; de Lacy 2002 (7d) [*ka'.ı'] 'to eat', [*tı,ku] 'louse'); Herrera 2014: first mora of the word.
1961.prule: Word stress (longer vowel, higher allotone of high tone, may be louder; de Lacy: greater duration and higher pitch) falls on the couplet (the bimoraic stem) or on a post-couplet syllable (suffix/enclitic), never on a pre-couplet syllable (prefix/proclitic), at a position determined by TONE, not by weight, syllable count or morpheme identity. Pankratz & Pike 1967: 293 (own summary, excerpt grade; tones 1/2/3 = H/M/L): (a) the first couplet or post-couplet syllable with tone 1 contiguously followed by tone 3 (HL); (b) else the tone-2 syllable of a 23 (ML) sequence; (c) else the first tone 1 (H) of the couplet or post-couplet; (d) else the first syllable of the couplet. de Lacy 1999 fn. 19 and 2002 (7a-d) reorder (b) and (c) to HL > H > ML > leftmost, because P&P's own data (ML*H [ku,nu' *ra!] 'his tobacco', 291.1) show a bare H attracting stress away from an ML sequence. P&P limit the rule: 'Word-stress is predictable by tone provided that the couplet occurs word-initially, but it is not predictable if the couplet occurs elsewhere.' Herrera 2014 (Coscatlán) states only the default: word accent 'suele estar en la primera mora'.

tn.translation: The language has five tones, borne mainly by vowels. Four occur in citation forms: high, low, falling, rising. The fifth, the mid tone, is felt only in syntax. ... Of the five tones recorded, two have a distinctive function: the high and low tones. They are the basic tones of the language. ... There are two tonemes in the language: a high toneme and a low toneme. ... Bàlòŋ is a floating-tone language. ... These floating tones act on the fixed tones. On the surface they create the modulated tones HB and BH as well as the mid tone.

1967.prule: Accent ('accent d'intensité') is assigned by morpheme class, not counted from a word edge: it is borne by the nominal or verbal radical (together with any derivational suffixes / postposed aspect markers) and by a listed set of grammatical morphemes (personal modalities, class-agreeing determiners, autonomous lexical items such as adverbs and independent numerals, functionals/propositives/preposed verbal modalities, class indices of type III 'pronominal' and type IV 'connective'); noun-class and verbal prefixes are never accented (2003: 'affixes (always non-accented)'). Historically the accent sat on the first syllable of the radical and the unaccented second syllable dropped, so stems are now mostly monosyllabic; synchronically the accent is stem-initial/root-borne.
1967.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress described. tn.translation: The tone system. The language has three level tones (high: v́, mid: v̄, low: v̀) and two contour tones (rising low-high: v̌ and falling high-low: v̂), but it has a strong tendency to function as a two-tone language (the low/mid opposition is detectable only in final position and it tends to disappear among the young and town-dwellers). Bafia is characterised in particular by two phenomena: - tonal lowering, which affects every high tone placed after another high tone in an HLH sequence ... - the 'faille tonale' (downstep), i.e. an abrupt tonal lowering ...

1982.heavy: Attracts stress: a final syllable whose nucleus is a diphthong /aw/, /ay/, /uy/ 'dan varian atau bentuk kembarnya' (CVV-type) - though one of the three printed examples, [uŋkay], carries no accent. Repels stress: a penult whose nucleus is /ə/ (stress goes to the final: [betám]; the second example [kantoŋ] is printed without an accent). Closed CVC finals are NOT heavy ([púlun] 'bungkus' keeps penult stress). Additional non-weight condition: onsetless V-initial disyllables (VCV(C)) take final stress.
1982.dflt: penult ('umumnya jatuh pada suku kedua dari belakang': [bányu], [káka], [púlun])
1982.prule: Word stress is non-phonemic. Regular stress 'generally' (umumnya) falls on the penult ([bányu], [káka], [púlun]; a closed CVC final does not attract). It moves to the final syllable when (1) the final syllable's nucleus is a diphthong /aw, ay, uy/ ([babáw], [lulúy]; the middle example /ukay/ is printed [uŋkay] with no accent); (2) the penult nucleus is schwa /ə/ (/bətam/ [betám]; the second example /kəntoŋ/ is printed [kantoŋ] with no accent); (3) a disyllable begins with a bare-V syllable, VCV(C) ([aják], [idúp], [umíh]). (4) In CVVCV(C) words (vowel sequence in antepenult+penult) the prose says stress 'may fall on the third or the second syllable from the end', but the printed examples mark penult vs final ([kuíni] ~ [kuiní], [kuítan] ~ [kuitán], [buáya] ~ [buayá]) - a source-internal inconsistency; either way this class is variable. Irregular (morphological) cases: suffixes -an/-i/-(a)kan 'often' (sering) draw stress onto the suffix syllable ([bálum] > [balumán], [búlik] > [bulikí], [múak] > [muakakán]); possessive enclitics -ku/-nya 'always' (selalu) take stress when word-final ([rumah] > [rumahkú], [rumahñá]). In phrases stress 'often' shifts to the following word; the phrase examples [rumah], [rumah ganal], [rumah naŋ ganal] are printed without accent marks.

1985.prule: Tone language: three level tones (high, mid, low) and two contour tones (rising, falling), lexically contrastive (minimal sets) and subject to complex tonal sandhi (Creissels 2025). No word-stress position is stated in any modern description. The specialist prosodic monograph (Ahoua 1996, known through its JALL 21 reviewer) argues that Baule is a tone language and not an accent language, the earlier accent classification being an artefact of isolation-form tonal neutralisation, with a rhythmic weak/strong alternation of tones organised in right-headed feet.
1985.srule: Not mentioned in Creissels 2025, Phonologie du baoulé, §4 Prosodie (pp. 1-3 read in full): the prosody section describes tone only (three level and two contour tones, tonal sandhi); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described in any modern source read (Creissels 2025 fiche langue; Leben & Ahoua 1997 abstract, 2006; Ahoua 1996 per JALL 21 review, which treats Baule rhythm as weak/strong TONAL alternation in right-headed feet, not stress).

vlen.q: Le baoulé a les types de syllabes suivants: N (nasale), V (voyelle), CV (consonne+voyelle) et CCV (consonne-consonne-voyelle). On note l’absence totale de syllabes fermées (càd. terminées par une consonne, cf. Fr. bac, bar, balle etc.).

tn.quote: Le baoulé est une langue à tons, avec comme particularité notable un système particulièrement complexe de règles de combinatoire tonale selon lesquelles la réalisation du ton porté par une syllabe est influencée par les tons des syllabes adjacentes. Le système tonal du baoulé oppose trois tons ponctuels (haut, moyen et bas) et deux tons modulés (montant et descendant). Les séries de mots suivantes illustrent la pertinence de ces distinctions tonales: ... sá ‘main’ ... sǎ ‘gingembre’ ... sâ ‘affaire’ ... blā ‘femme’ ... blâ ‘puits’ ... sìn ‘dos’ ... sîn ‘feu’
tn.translation: Baule is a tone language, with as a notable peculiarity a particularly complex system of tonal combination rules by which the realisation of the tone borne by a syllable is influenced by the tones of adjacent syllables. The tonal system of Baule opposes three level tones (high, mid and low) and two contour tones (rising and falling). The following word series illustrate the relevance of these tonal distinctions: ... sá 'hand' ... sǎ 'ginger' ... sâ 'matter' ... blā 'woman' ... blâ 'well' ... sìn 'back' ... sîn 'fire'
tn.cite: Creissels, Denis. 2025. Phonologie du baoulé. Fiche phonologique LGIDF/LGMEF (DDL/Université Lyon 2, CNRS), hal-05002378v1, 3 pp.; companion fiche 'Le baoulé' (4 pp., same deposit)
tn.note: Five tonemes: H, M, L plus rising and falling, shown in a 26-word minimal-set table; complex tone sandhi; companion fiche adds toneless clitics and TAM marked by tone; nothing on stress or downstep.

1986.prule: Word accent falls on the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable of the host word: antepenultimate 'ordinairement' when the word carries the weak terminals -tsy or -ky (Bara reflexes of Merina -tra/-ka), otherwise penultimate; the terminals -tsy/-ky may be kept or dropped at the speaker's discretion. Suffixation moves the radical's accent one syllable to the right ('accent du radical sur la syllabe suivante'). Faublée 1947: accent placement can be stated by fixed rules ('règles fixes'); the accented vowel is also long; accented i becomes e. No syllable-count rule is stated; the conditioning is the segmental identity of the final syllable (weak terminals), not weight.
1986.srule: Only at group level in the pages seen: the proclitic articles/deictics (ny; ley, lei) are unaccented or 'ne portent qu'un accent secondaire', the 'accent principal' falling on the determined noun (NY renibe, LEY ólo). No word-internal secondary-stress placement appears in the excerpt seen; the accent-rule page (index 'Pénultième, 46') is unseen.
